claim: Blind expert reviewers rated LLM-generated research ideas as more novel than human expert ideas, and slightly less feasible (novelty 5.64 vs 4.84, feasibility 6.34 vs 6.61).
quote: LLM-generated ideas are judged as more novel (p < 0.05) than human expert ideas
title: Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
transfer: Novelty is easy for an LLM to reach; the agent's bottleneck is feasibility and selection, so spend budget on checking, not on more novelty.

claim: Generating 4000 ideas per topic left only about 200 unique ones (about 5%) after dedup at cosine similarity 0.8: single-model samples repeat heavily.
title: Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
transfer: Add an embedding dedup step after divergent sampling; count only distinct ideas toward the budget.

claim: LLM judges were near chance at ranking ideas: best Claude pairwise ranker agreed with human review ranking 53.3% of the time, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%, versus 56.1% human inter-reviewer agreement.
title: Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
transfer: Do not let the same model rank its own ideas as the final selector; prefer an external check (run, test, retrieval) over LLM judgment.

claim: After 43 experts spent 100+ hours executing ideas, AI ideas lost about 1.05 novelty points and 1.98 overall points, human ideas almost none; the ranking flipped on many metrics.
quote: the scores of the LLM-generated ideas decrease significantly more than expert-written ideas on all evaluation metrics
title: The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
transfer: Novelty judged on paper is not outcome. Route every promising idea through an execution or prototype step before it is trusted.

claim: Before execution AI ideas were rated more novel (5.78 vs 4.91); after execution novelty was equal (4.73 vs 4.90). Reviewers found flaws only once results were visible.
title: The Ideation-Execution Gap
transfer: Late, evidence-based critique beats early opinion critique; delay the verdict on novelty until a result exists.

claim: Giving writers GPT-4 story ideas raised novelty (+5.4% with 1 idea, +8.1% with 5) and usefulness (+3.7%, +9.0%) but made stories more similar to each other.
quote: generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
transfer: One agent calling itself repeatedly will converge. Each divergent call needs a different seed or constraint, and diversity should be measured across calls.

claim: Users with ChatGPT produced less semantically distinct ideas than users of another tool, and felt less responsible for them.
title: Homogenization Effects of Large Language Models on Human Creative Ideation
transfer: Anchoring on the first model output narrows search; write the agent's own independent attempt before showing it any prior output.

claim: LLM responses on standard creativity tests are much more similar to each other than human responses are to each other, across many models.
quote: LLM responses are much more similar to other LLM responses than human responses are to each other
title: We're Different, We're the Same: Creative Homogeneity Across LLMs
transfer: A second model call is not independent; diversity must be forced through structure (different frames, constraints, retrieval), not resampling.

claim: Language models show an Artificial Hivemind effect: one model repeats itself and different models give strikingly similar outputs on open-ended queries; LM judges align less with humans when humans disagree.
authors: Jiang, Chai, Li, Liu, Fok, Dziri, Tsvetkov, Sap, Albalak, Choi
title: Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond)
n: 26K queries, 31,250 human annotations, 25 raters per item
transfer: Do not treat agreement among samples as evidence of novelty or correctness; use judge disagreement as a signal to search wider.

claim: Across 14 LLMs, only 0.28% of responses reached the top 10% of human creativity benchmarks, and the same model with the same prompt ranged from below average to original.
quote: no evidence of increased creative performance
title: Has the Creativity of Large-Language Models peaked?
transfer: Within-model variance is large, so many cheap draws followed by selection is a legitimate way to reach rare high-originality outputs.

claim: LLM judges rate model-generated research questions as highly novel (the novelty mirage) while domain experts prefer author-anchored reference questions.
title: RQ-Bench: On the Limits of LLM-as-Judge for Scientific Novelty Assessment
transfer: An LLM novelty score cannot be the reward for selecting ideas; anchor novelty to retrieval of prior work and to expert-like checks.

claim: Time-split evaluation: scores based on real future citations and acceptance correlated negatively with LLM-judged novelty (rho -0.29), and retrieval-augmented generation scored 2.5x higher on real impact though an LLM judge saw no difference.
title: HindSight: Evaluating LLM-Generated Research Ideas via Future Impact
transfer: Ground ideas in retrieved prior literature before generating; do not select on novel-sounding wording.

claim: On the Alternate Uses Task, LLM raters preferred AI responses over human ones, but the bias vanished once idea elaboration was controlled.
title: The Effect of Idea Elaboration on the Automatic Assessment of Idea Originality
transfer: Normalise length and detail of candidate ideas before any LLM comparison, or the judge rewards verbosity.

claim: A framework that retrieves concepts across abstraction levels to link distant fields, then decomposes and recombines them, produced ideas closer to later real research (similarity up about 7-10%) on OAG-Bench.
title: LLMs can realize combinatorial creativity: generating creative ideas via LLMs for scientific research
transfer: Agent step: split a problem into parts at several abstraction levels, retrieve from a distant field per part, recombine. Similarity to later work is a weak outcome measure.

claim: Scideator extracts purpose, mechanism and evaluation facets from papers, retrieves analogous work at controlled distance, and recombines facets; users reported significantly more creativity support than a same-LLM baseline.
quote: significantly more creativity support than a baseline using the same backbone LLM
authors: Radensky, Shahid, Fok, Siangliulue, Hope, Weld
title: Scideator: Human-LLM Scientific Idea Generation Grounded in Research-Paper Facet Recombination
n: user study of CS researchers; count not on abstract page
transfer: Facet recombination is a concrete Uzzi-style step: split into purpose and mechanism, swap one facet from a far source. Measures perceived support, not outcome quality; human-in-loop in the original.

claim: AutoDiscovery uses Bayesian surprise (shift from prior to posterior belief after an experiment) as reward in tree search; it found 5-29% more LLM-surprising discoveries than competitors on 21 datasets, and about two-thirds were also surprising to experts.
authors: Agarwal et al. (author list not captured)
title: AutoDiscovery: Open-ended Scientific Discovery via Bayesian Surprise
transfer: Anomaly step: state a prior prediction, run the check, and treat large belief shifts as the cue to branch the search.

claim: With thinking enabled, LLMs on bandit tasks move toward human-like mixes of random and directed exploration; in changing environments they adapt worse, especially in directed exploration.
title: LLMs vs humans vs bandit algorithms on the exploration-exploitation tradeoff
transfer: Do not rely on the model to balance explore and exploit itself; set the switch in the program (fixed explore phase, then exploit).

claim: LLMs are useful for exploring large semantically rich action spaces by proposing candidates but exploit poorly: all tested LLMs did worse than simple linear regression on bandits, even with tool use or summarisation.
title: Should You Use Your Large Language Model to Explore or Exploit?
transfer: Let the LLM propose candidates (explore) and let code or statistics score and pick (exploit).

claim: Most LLMs struggle to explore a partially hidden state space when exploration is the only goal; exploration performance rises with reasoning ability.
quote: most struggle to explore the state space
title: Disentangling Exploration of Large Language Models by Optimal Exploitation
transfer: Force coverage: keep an explicit list of unexplored options and require the next step to pick from it.

claim: On creative problem solving with functional fixedness (1,600+ problems), GPT-4 single-try 62.4% vs humans 65.1%; best-of-many GPT-4 92.3%. Divergent-convergent prompting raised efficient solutions 6.5%; step-wise reflection cut infeasible solutions 9.7%.
quote: MACGYVER is challenging for both groups, but in unique and complementary ways.
title: MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
transfer: Pair a divergent step with a feasibility reflection step; the gap between average and best-of-many shows selection has more headroom than generation.

claim: Papers with first-time combinations of referenced journals show delayed recognition, are more often top 1% cited in the long run, have higher variance, and are cited more in foreign fields.
quote: strong evidence of delayed recognition of novel papers
title: Bias against novelty in science: A cautionary tale for users of bibliometric indicators
transfer: Early signals undervalue breakthroughs. Do not drop a distant-combination idea on a short-horizon score alone; keep a small protected slot for high-variance ideas. The funding-bias part applies to organisations only. Pre-2018, listed for context.

claim: Uzzi et al. scored 17.9 million papers: highest-impact work combines mostly conventional knowledge with a small dose of novel pairs; papers only novel or only conventional rarely reached top citations; teams inject novelty more than solo authors.
title: Atypical Combinations and Scientific Impact
transfer: Mix rule for the agent: anchor most of a solution in well-tested parts and add one or two distant parts. The team result applies to teams only. Pre-2018, for context; no replication found in my searches (search budget ran out).
